partial.content:
A hash table is a way of storing information so that a particular key can usually be found quickly. You can picture it as an array of numbered slots, often called buckets. Each bucket is a place where one or more entries may live. An entry normally contains a key and its associated value, so the table is not merely a set of keys; it is a collection of key-value pairs. To find the value for a key, the table first turns that key into a number using a hash function. That number is then reduced to a bucket index, commonly by taking the remainder after division by the number of buckets. The lookup goes to that bucket and searches the entries stored there for one whose key matches the key being sought. If it finds the key, it returns the associated value; if it reaches the end of the bucket’s entries without finding the key, the key is absent from the table.

A hash function is a deterministic procedure that maps a key to a number. Deterministic means the same key always produces the same hash value within a given table, which is essential because otherwise a lookup could go to the wrong bucket. A useful hash function also spreads different keys across the available buckets as evenly as possible, while being fast to compute. It need not produce a unique number for every possible key, and in general it cannot do so when there are more possible keys than buckets. When two different keys map to the same bucket, that is called a collision. Collisions are normal and must be handled by the table rather than treated as a failure.

The common collision-handling method described here is chaining. With chaining, each bucket does not hold just one entry; it holds a collection of entries, often a linked list or a small array. All entries whose keys hash to the same bucket are placed in that bucket’s collection. A lookup therefore has two stages. First it computes the hash and chooses the bucket. Then it walks through the entries in that bucket, comparing each stored key with the sought key. If a bucket contains only one entry, the second stage is trivial. If it contains several, the lookup may compare several keys before finding the right one. The comparisons are necessary because different keys can share a bucket.

Consider a small made-up example. Suppose a table has six buckets numbered zero through five. Pretend, purely for illustration and not as a real hash function, that the invented hash assigns cedar to bucket two, maple to bucket two, and pine to bucket five. When cedar is inserted, bucket two contains cedar. When maple is inserted, its hash also points to bucket two, so maple is added to the same bucket, producing a chain containing cedar and maple. Pine goes alone into bucket five. To look up maple, the table computes the pretended hash, arrives at bucket two, and examines the chain there. It compares the first entry, cedar, which does not match maple, then compares the second entry, maple, which does match, and returns maple’s value. To look up pine, it goes directly to bucket five and finds pine there. If a key such as oak were made-up to hash to bucket two, a lookup would inspect cedar and maple, find neither match, and conclude that oak is not present in the table. This example shows both the basic route to a bucket and the extra work caused by a collision.

The efficiency of lookup depends strongly on how many entries each bucket holds. A useful measure is the load factor, defined as the number of stored entries divided by the number of buckets. If the table has a load factor near one, the average bucket contains roughly one entry. If the load factor is ten, the average bucket contains about ten entries, so an unsuccessful lookup may have to compare many keys before giving up. To keep chains short, a hash table typically resizes when the load factor rises above a chosen threshold. Resizing allocates a larger array of buckets and then reinserts every existing entry by recomputing its hash for the new bucket count. This rehashing redistributes entries
